summary: RFC 3723 specified IPsec requirements for block storage protocols over IP such as iSCSI, based on IPsec v2. This document updates those requirements for IPsec v3.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC updates security requirements for iSCSI and related block-storage protocols. It adds IPsec v3 guidance and changes which encryption algorithms and key-management features implementations need to support.

questions: why was 3des replaced by aes cbc for storage
extended sequence numbers esp high speed
subtitle: Updated IPsec requirements for iSCSI and other block-storage protocols, including newer algorithms.

tldr.problem: RFC 3723 specified IPsec requirements for block-storage protocols using IPsec v2. Its requirements needed updates for IPsec v3 and changes in cryptography.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends support for IPsec v3 and IKEv2, requires extended sequence numbers for implementations operating at 1 gigabit/second or higher, and makes AES CBC the mandatory confidentiality transform.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7146 updates the IPsec requirements of RFC 3723 and protocols that adopted them. It also changes requirements for key management, authentication and certificate checking.

facts.label: Extended sequence numbers
facts.value: 64 bits; required at 1 gigabit/second or higher

today: RFC 7146 is a Standards Track document published in April 2014. It updates RFC 3723 and other RFCs that adopted its IPsec requirements; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates RFC 7146.

sections.title: Why RFC 3723 Needed an Update
sections.content:
RFC 3723 defines IPsec requirements for block-storage protocols over IP, such as iSCSI. Other specifications later reused those requirements, including remote direct data placement protocols. RFC 7146 updates the requirements for IPsec v3 and reflects developments in cryptography.

IPsec v2 remains a requirement to preserve interoperability with existing implementations. IPsec v3, including ESPv3 and IKEv2, should also be implemented. The RFC expects block-storage protocols to operate at high data rates, which affects sequence-number and cipher requirements.

The updates apply to RFC 3723 and to protocols that use its IPsec requirements. The RFC identifies which related specifications are covered and excludes documents whose use of RFC 3723 does not involve those requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier storage-security requirements were written for IPsec v2. This RFC updates them for IPsec v3 and for the higher data rates expected of storage traffic.

sections.title: ESP and Extended Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 3723 requires ESPv2 in tunnel mode, with data-origin authentication, integrity and replay protection for each packet. RFC 7146 says implementations should also support ESPv3 in tunnel mode and requires the same protections when ESPv3 is used.

ESP's 32-bit sequence number cannot wrap within one security association. Implementations capable of operating at 1 gigabit/second or higher MUST implement extended 64-bit sequence numbers for ESPv2 and, if supported, ESPv3. They SHOULD use extended sequence numbers for all block-storage protocol traffic.

HMAC-SHA-1-96 remains required for integrity. AES CBC MAC with XCBC extensions should be supported with 128-bit keys. Implementations supporting IKEv2 should also support AES GMAC with 128-bit keys.
sections.plainLanguage: Fast storage links can exhaust a 32-bit packet sequence number quickly. The RFC requires a 64-bit sequence-number option for implementations that can operate at 1 gigabit/second or faster.

sections.title: Confidentiality Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 7146 changes the implementation requirements for confidentiality transforms. AES CBC with 128-bit keys becomes MUST implement. 3DES CBC and AES Counter mode become MAY implement. Implementations supporting IKEv2 should also implement AES GCM with 128-bit keys. NULL encryption remains a MUST, allowing authentication and integrity without confidentiality.

The RFC lowers the requirement for 3DES CBC because its 64-bit block size reaches a birthday bound of 32 GiB. At high data rates, this can require frequent rekeying. AES has a 128-bit block size and a birthday bound of 2^68 bytes.

AES CTR is no longer the transform considered most suitable for hardware implementation; the RFC assigns that role to AES GCM, which combines encryption and integrity protection. The requirement change for AES CTR is based on hardware considerations, not a change in its security properties.
sections.plainLanguage: AES CBC becomes the required encryption transform, while 3DES CBC and AES CTR become optional. The change reduces the rekeying pressure associated with 3DES's smaller block size.

sections.title: IKE, Key Sizes and Rekeying
sections.content:
IKEv1 remains required for authentication, security-association negotiation and key management. IKEv2 should also be supported. Manual keying MUST NOT be used with any IPsec version covered by the RFC because it does not provide the rekeying support needed at high data rates.

When Diffie-Hellman groups are used, proposals should offer a group of at least 2048 bits. Use of 1024-bit groups is not recommended. The requirement to use UDP port 500 for IKEv1 is removed to allow NAT traversal.

The RFC also extends the perfect-forward-secrecy requirement to the IKEv2 CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange. Deleting a security association should not by itself tear down the storage connection; a new association can protect later traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers negotiate keys with IKE rather than entering keys manually. The RFC recommends IKEv2 and larger Diffie-Hellman groups, and requires support for perfect forward secrecy in the named exchanges.

sections.title: Peer Authentication and Certificate Checks
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support peer authentication with a pre-shared cryptographic key. They MAY support certificate-based authentication with digital signatures. When signatures are used, negotiators should request certificates and check validity through a CRL or OCSP before accepting them.

The RFC specifies identity types that IKEv1 and IKEv2 implementations must support, including IPv4 addresses, IPv6 addresses when supported by the protocol stack, and fully qualified domain names. The opaque ID_KEY_ID type MUST NOT be used because it does not interoperate consistently among IPsec implementations.

IKEv1 must support Main Mode and should support Aggressive Mode. Main Mode with a pre-shared key should not be used when an endpoint has a dynamically assigned IP address, because this requires a group key and creates a man-in-the-middle risk.
sections.plainLanguage: Peers must authenticate each other using a shared key, and may use certificates. The RFC also specifies which identity forms to support and warns against a group-key setup with dynamic addresses.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is entirely about security requirements. It calls attention to the changed requirement levels for AES CBC, AES GCM, AES GMAC, 3DES CBC and AES CTR. It says AES GCM and AES GMAC are vulnerable to catastrophic forgery if a nonce is repeated with the same key.

3DES CBC remains optional and may suit implementations operating at lower speeds where its rekeying frequency is acceptable. AES CTR also remains optional and suitable for general use, although AES GCM is favored for hardware implementation.

Cryptographic algorithms and transforms used within one security association should use key sizes of comparable strength. Security considerations from the referenced IPsec and cryptographic RFCs also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: AES GCM and GMAC require careful nonce handling: reusing a nonce with the same key can enable serious forgery attacks. Other IPsec security requirements still apply.
